nano_site.science.description: Draft conceptual scientific figures with structured Nano Banana prompts. Plan panels and arrows, verify labels, separate real data and keep editable sources.
nano_site.science.heading: Nano Banana 2.1 for scientific figures
nano_site.science.intro: Prepare a conceptual schematic that a subject expert can inspect. Plan the entities, arrows and labels first, then build the final figure around verified science.
nano_site.science.section_0.title: Separate a conceptual diagram from a data figure
nano_site.science.section_0.body:
A workflow, apparatus overview or graphical summary can explain an idea without reporting a measurement. State that purpose in the brief and caption. List the relationships the reader should understand, such as the order of sample preparation, measurement and review.

A measured curve must come from the dataset and its analysis. Microscopy, gel bands and experimental observations must come from the actual experiment. Keep those source files and their processing history separate from the illustration. If exact dimensions or geometry carry scientific meaning, construct them in an appropriate drawing or plotting tool.
nano_site.science.section_1.title: Write a structured scientific-figure prompt
nano_site.science.section_1.body:
Use this structure: purpose; entities or stages; allowed connections; exact labels; layout; styling; excluded content. For a four-stage workflow, place sample preparation, measurement, analysis and review in that order, with arrows only between adjacent stages. Ask for consistent shapes and room for a caption.

Define ambiguous relationships explicitly. State whether an arrow means sequence, transport, activation or inhibition, and use the convention accepted in your field. If the subject needs a legend, list its symbols and meanings. Ask for a clean conceptual draft without invented measurements, error bars or microscopic textures.
nano_site.science.section_2.title: Audit every label and arrow manually
nano_site.science.section_2.body:
Create a label list from verified terminology before generating. Match each finished label against that list character by character, including Greek letters, superscripts, units and capitalization. Check that every arrow starts and ends at the intended entity and that its direction communicates the right relationship.

Then inspect for added structures, omitted steps and visual cues that imply unsupported scale or evidence. A subject expert should approve the content before style changes. Replace labels in an editable text layer and repeat the review at the planned print or slide size; a correct word that becomes unreadable still needs correction.
nano_site.science.section_3.title: Combine real plots with an approved schematic
nano_site.science.section_3.body:
Export real-data plots from the analysis tool with clear axes, units and the appropriate uncertainty representation. Assemble them with the reviewed schematic in a layout tool, retaining each original source. Give panels stable letters and use the caption to state what each panel represents.

Keep line widths, colors and label sizes consistent without changing the meaning of data. Do not request a generated redraw of a plot that would alter points or error bars. For a presentation, inspect it from a normal reading distance; for a paper, inspect a proof at its final column width.
nano_site.science.faq_0.question: Can Nano Banana create real scientific data?
nano_site.science.faq_0.answer: An image model cannot supply experimental observations. Use your actual data and validated analytical tools for measurements and plots; use this recipe for conceptual explanation.
nano_site.science.faq_1.question: How do I make scientific labels reliable?
nano_site.science.faq_1.answer: Build a verified label list, compare every character, check units and arrow relationships, and typeset final labels manually in an editable layer. Have a subject expert review the completed figure.
nano_site.editor.title: Nano Banana 2.1 Editor: Plan Reference Image Edits
nano_site.editor.description: Prepare a Nano Banana reference edit: preview images, state changes and preservation rules, choose a shape and check model readiness before generating.
nano_site.editor.heading: Nano Banana 2.1 image editor
nano_site.editor.intro: Keep what works. Change the part you can describe. Preview your reference locally and write a preservation list before requesting an edit.
nano_site.editor.section_0.title: Make one clear edit
nano_site.editor.section_0.body:
A good first edit changes the background, color palette, light direction or a specific object. State the change directly and list the elements that must stay unchanged. Include the camera angle and crop when they matter.

Avoid describing a full redesign when you want a small correction. If the face, product shape or exact text is important, make that part of the preservation list. Review the returned image against the list, not only against its overall appearance.
nano_site.editor.section_1.title: Understand local preview and upload
nano_site.editor.section_1.body:
Sign in and add a reference image. The control uploads required files and shows when they are ready. Describe the change, choose the model and review the quote before submitting the edit.

Use only images you own or have permission to process. Remove material unnecessary for the task. If you replace a reference, check the prompt again.
nano_site.editor.section_2.title: Keep a repeatable version history
nano_site.editor.section_2.body:
Save the original reference, prompt, selected model and result together. Make the next request a correction to one observed problem. For example, “restore the original label position; keep the new background.”

Name each saved brief by its task and version. A clean record helps a collaborator continue the work and lets you stop when the image meets the brief, rather than iterating without a decision rule.
nano_site.editor.section_3.title: Know when to use a manual tool
nano_site.editor.section_3.body:
Use manual layers for exact lettering, product dimensions, legal disclosures and final layout alignment. Generative edits can propose visual directions, but they do not replace precise typesetting or verified geometry.

Our existing tool directory includes additional editing workflows. If you move from this brief to a different tool, check its selected model and cost again. Saving a prompt does not authorize an automatic paid request.
nano_site.editor.faq_0.question: Does previewing upload my file?
nano_site.editor.faq_0.answer: For a reference edit, images are uploaded so the model can process them. The reference control shows upload progress before submission.
nano_site.editor.faq_1.question: Can the editor guarantee unchanged text?
nano_site.editor.faq_1.answer: No. Verify every important letter and add final text in a manual editable layer when precision matters.
nano_site.guide.title: How to Use Nano Banana 2.1: Prompt, Edit & Review
nano_site.guide.description: Prepare your first Nano Banana 2.1 image: choose a task, write a brief, add references and review text and identity before saving the final result.
nano_site.guide.heading: How to use Nano Banana 2.1, one task at a time
nano_site.guide.intro: Begin with a single product image, poster or background edit. This workflow helps you prepare a clear request and decide whether a result is ready to use.
nano_site.guide.section_0.title: 1. Define the destination and the finished image
nano_site.guide.section_0.body:
Write one sentence describing where the image will appear: a square catalog card, a portrait event poster or a wide website header. Choose the shape and leave space for any final text. List the details you will check, such as a readable headline or an unchanged product label.

Pick the closest recipe in the prompt library and replace its subject. Keep the first brief simple enough to evaluate. One product and one lighting direction are easier to inspect than a crowded scene with several characters and text blocks.
nano_site.guide.section_1.title: 2. Choose the model and check access
nano_site.guide.section_1.body:
Sign in, choose Nano Banana 2.1 or another connected model, and review the credit quote. Nano Banana 2.1 generates or edits one 1K image for 8 credits per request.

The current email-and-password flow does not require email verification. Stripe checkout lets you purchase a monthly membership or credit pack; your balance and billing records are available in your account.
nano_site.guide.section_2.title: 3. Describe the scene or prepare a reference edit
nano_site.guide.section_2.body:
For a new image, specify subject, composition, lighting and exact text. For an edit, state the change and then list what must remain: identity, geometry, label, camera angle and crop. Explain the role of each reference rather than expecting the model to infer it.

Check the images for details that contradict your prompt. If the original has a white cap and the brief says blue cap, decide which requirement is intended before proceeding. Use files you have permission to process and remove confidential material that the task does not need.
nano_site.guide.section_3.title: 4. Submit once and follow the task
nano_site.guide.section_3.body:
When the selected workflow is available, wait for required uploads to finish and check the quote again after changing output settings. Submit one request and follow its status. If it is slow, keep the task identifier instead of repeatedly starting the same job.

A timeout can leave uncertainty about whether the provider accepted the request. Check the existing task before retrying. Developers should retain the returned queue identifier and use documented status and response URLs; the API guide gives the same principle without requiring you to expose a credential in the browser.
nano_site.guide.faq_0.question: What should a beginner try first?
nano_site.guide.faq_0.answer: Choose one product photo or a simple background edit. Set a single output shape and write a short list of details that must be right.
nano_site.guide.faq_1.question: Do I need an account just to prepare a prompt?
nano_site.guide.faq_1.answer: No. You can write, copy and download a brief without an account. Available generation workflows require their displayed sign-in and credit conditions.
nano_site.migration.title: Nano Banana 2 to 2.1 Migration: Test Before Switching
nano_site.migration.description: Migrate from Nano Banana 2 to 2.1 with acceptance tests, verified endpoints, cost checks and a rollback plan. Check lifecycle notices before switching.
nano_site.migration.heading: Nano Banana 2 to 2.1: a controlled migration
nano_site.migration.intro: Keep a working baseline while you evaluate the replacement. A migration should preserve the tasks your users depend on, with clear model labels and a way to pause the rollout.
nano_site.migration.section_0.title: Inventory the workflow you already rely on
nano_site.migration.section_0.body:
Record the actual provider endpoint and model identifier, input fields, reference files, output formats and billing assumptions. Keep a few representative successful tasks and common failures. Include exact lettering, a product edit and a simple new-image brief so the acceptance set covers different demands.

Save raw outputs and note any manual fixes. Agree which requirements must remain after migration: supported shape, product preservation, complete download or a maximum task cost. This gives you a baseline that can be checked without relying on memory or a demo selected for its appearance.
nano_site.migration.section_1.title: Test 2.1 with a separate integration
nano_site.migration.section_1.body:
Use the documented 2.1 endpoint and verify its input contract instead of changing only the label in a model menu. Confirm the allowed settings, reference handling and returned files before routing existing work through it. Keep each task's actual model identifier visible in your records.

Run the acceptance set under comparable settings and inspect the same criteria. Record quotes, failed requests and correction effort alongside output quality. If an option differs, adjust the application deliberately and repeat the affected test; do not silently carry an old reference limit or price into the new workflow.
nano_site.migration.section_2.title: Roll out gradually and define the fallback
nano_site.migration.section_2.body:
Start with a bounded portion of your own workflow or a small group that understands the test. Decide what will stop the rollout: a recurring identity error, incompatible output, or cost beyond the agreed limit. Keep task identifiers so failures can be investigated without creating duplicate requests.

Retain the previous workflow until the new one meets the acceptance criteria. A fallback must identify which model actually produced the image and whether another request has a cost. Returning an older model's output under a 2.1 label would make later review and billing decisions unreliable.
nano_site.migration.section_3.title: Use official lifecycle notices to schedule the switch
nano_site.migration.section_3.body:
The official Google table reviewed on October 10, 2026 lists Nano Banana 2.1 as the recommended replacement for gemini-3.1-flash-image, but does not announce a shutdown date for that stable model. An October 29 deadline should therefore not drive a forced migration.

Check the current lifecycle documentation and your provider's release notes before changing production use. Keep the review date and acceptance record with the integration. If a confirmed notice changes the deadline or supported options, update the affected tests and tell users which workflow remains available.
nano_site.migration.faq_0.question: Is a migration required by October 29, 2026?
nano_site.migration.faq_0.answer: No such deadline is announced for gemini-3.1-flash-image in the official table reviewed on October 10, 2026. Recheck the linked documentation for later changes.
nano_site.migration.faq_1.question: Can I migrate by renaming the model selector?
nano_site.migration.faq_1.answer: No. Verify the endpoint, input fields, output processing, request status and cost. A different display label does not change which model receives a task.
nano_site.pro.title: Nano Banana Pro: Reference Editing & Model Guide
nano_site.pro.description: Prepare Nano Banana Pro generation and reference edits. Compare Pro with 2.1, write preservation instructions and check the model-specific credit quote.
nano_site.pro.heading: Nano Banana Pro for a more deliberate image
nano_site.pro.intro: The Pro workflow belongs on its own page. Prepare a demanding composition or reference edit, then compare the result against the same brief used for 2.1.
nano_site.pro.section_0.title: Give Pro a concrete brief
nano_site.pro.section_0.body:
Describe the required output, not a vague request for “professional quality.” Specify the subject, hierarchy, lighting and exact wording. For a complex composition, say which elements are essential and which can be simplified.

Google lists Pro separately from 2.1. This site selects its own documented provider endpoint when Pro is chosen. Check availability and credit pricing before a request; do not infer them from the 2.1 page.
nano_site.pro.section_1.title: Use references with defined roles
nano_site.pro.section_1.body:
Explain whether each reference supplies identity, product geometry, layout or visual style. Give a preservation list for the details that must survive an edit. Keep references focused rather than including every image from a project folder.

Inspect the result for introduced text, changed logos or altered proportions. A visually convincing image still needs a rights and accuracy review before commercial publication.
nano_site.pro.section_2.title: Compare with 2.1 using the same task
nano_site.pro.section_2.body:
Keep the prompt and reference set the same when comparing. Record actual outputs and costs instead of copying a quality score from another website. Our comparison guide gives you a repeatable checklist.

Choose the workflow that meets your important constraints with a workable review budget. Revisit the choice when your project changes from a poster to a product edit, or when provider options change.
nano_site.pro.section_3.title: Save the reusable parts
nano_site.pro.section_3.body:
Keep a successful prompt, the chosen model and the reference files with the final image. Note any manual corrections to lettering or geometry. That record helps another creator continue the work without guessing.

Use the editor for a specific correction and the prompt library for a new direction. Moving between tools should be intentional: confirm the selected model and quote whenever you start a new paid task.
nano_site.pro.faq_0.question: Does Pro always cost the same as 2.1?
nano_site.pro.faq_0.answer: No. Model quotes are separate. Read the current site quote or direct provider price for the exact workflow.
nano_site.pro.faq_1.question: Is this an official Pro website?
nano_site.pro.faq_1.answer: No. This is an independent workspace with links to official provider documentation.
nano_site.home.section_5.title: Nano Banana 2.1 prompt examples
nano_site.home.section_5.body:
A product brief can specify one bottle, a pale stone surface, soft light from the left and empty space above. A poster brief can supply a single headline in quotation marks and ask for a clear reading order. For an edit, write a direct instruction such as changing the background while preserving the original label and crop.

Use a recipe as a starting point and replace details that do not belong to your project. Save a baseline, then change one observed problem per revision. The prompt library includes product, poster, character, editing, storyboard and scientific schematic briefs.
nano_site.home.section_6.title: Understand pricing before choosing a plan
nano_site.home.section_6.body:
Monthly plans renew automatically; credit packs are one-time purchases valid for 365 days. Alipay prepaid membership lasts one month without automatic renewal. Review the product, amount and billing schedule on the checkout page.

Nano Banana 2.1 generation and reference editing use 8 credits per single-image 1K request. Other models have their own quotes. A failed provider task follows the credit reversal workflow; a completed image that does not match a creative preference is a different case.
nano_site.home.section_7.title: From product photos to scientific figures
nano_site.home.section_7.body:
Choose a reusable workflow for repeated work. A product catalog needs stable framing, a consistent background and recognizable packaging. Social posts need room for final copy; a character series needs a written identity checklist that can be checked across scenes.

Scientific figures need a different review. Use image generation to draft conceptual workflows or explanatory illustrations, then verify the relationships and add final labels in an editable layer. Measured plots and experimental imagery must come from real data; the scientific figures guide shows how to keep those roles separate.
nano_site.home.section_8.title: What can you do for free?
nano_site.home.section_8.body:
Writing, adapting, copying and downloading a prompt brief is free. Sign in to generate and use the balance displayed in your account.

Daily check-in and invitation rewards follow the account rules. They are credits, not unlimited generation. Email-and-password registration does not require email verification.
nano_site.home.section_9.title: API access and a controlled migration
nano_site.home.section_9.body:
Developers can use the API guide to plan direct fal integration with their own server-side credential. Keep the task identifier, follow its status and distinguish a pending task from a failed submission. This guide is not an offer of a public generation API operated by this site.

For an existing Nano Banana 2 workflow, inventory prompts, references and costs before switching. The official deprecation table reviewed on October 10, 2026 does not announce an October 29 shutdown for gemini-3.1-flash-image. Use a tested migration plan and current provider documentation rather than a countdown.
nano_site.home.faq_4.question: Can I use it for scientific figures?
nano_site.home.faq_4.answer: Use the workflow for conceptual schematics and explanatory illustrations. Create measured charts from your real data, then have a subject expert review relationships, labels and the final caption.
nano_site.home.faq_5.question: Is Nano Banana 2 shutting down on October 29?
nano_site.home.faq_5.answer: That date is not announced for gemini-3.1-flash-image in the official table reviewed on October 10, 2026. Check the linked lifecycle documentation before planning a forced switch.
nano_site.prompts.section_4.title: Turn a recipe into a repeatable revision
nano_site.prompts.section_4.body:
Replace the recipe's subject, destination shape and material before adding decorative style. Keep a baseline copy and give revisions useful names, such as bottle-background-v2. Write down the one defect you are fixing: a misplaced label, crowded title or missing contact shadow.

Save the prompt with the selected model and references. These recipes are original creative briefs, not a set of measured 2.1 outputs. Nano Banana 2.1 generation is not enabled here yet; you can still adapt, copy and download the instructions without credits.
nano_site.prompts.faq_2.question: How should I prompt a reference edit?
nano_site.prompts.faq_2.answer: Name what must change and what must remain. Explain the role of every reference and review identity, geometry, labels and crop against the original image.
nano_site.comparison.section_4.title: Choose for a workflow, then retain the evidence
nano_site.comparison.section_4.body:
A successful product edit can justify reusing a model for similar catalog work. A poster result needs its own review because lettering and layout introduce different failure modes. If the brief changes, repeat the relevant check instead of carrying over a general winner label.

Keep the prompt, model identifier, references, settings, raw outputs and review notes together. The Pro guide helps prepare demanding edits; the Nano Banana 2 migration guide helps compare an existing baseline with 2.1. Your decision becomes more useful when another person can reproduce its conditions.
nano_site.comparison.faq_2.question: Are the images on this site a benchmark?
nano_site.comparison.faq_2.answer: No. Workflow illustrations and original prompt recipes are not a measured 2.1-versus-Pro test. Only outputs produced by the explicitly named model can support a result comparison.
nano_site.science.section_4.title: Retain an editable source and a review record
nano_site.science.section_4.body:
Save the brief, selected model, source references, illustration draft and final layout together. Note which labels were added manually and who reviewed the scientific relationships. Use a caption that identifies the conceptual role of the illustration rather than implying an observation.

Before submission, check the destination's current image and disclosure requirements. A generated draft is not automatically publication-ready. Nano Banana 2.1 generation is not enabled in this workbench yet; the structured recipe remains available to copy, adapt and take into a separately available workflow.
nano_site.science.faq_2.question: Can I submit a generated schematic to a journal?
nano_site.science.faq_2.answer: Check that journal's current requirements, verify the science and preserve the editable source and disclosure record. This guide does not guarantee acceptance or publication readiness.
nano_site.guide.section_4.title: 5. Review the result and save a usable version
nano_site.guide.section_4.body:
Open the result at the size where it will be used. Read every word, compare identity and product details with the references, and check the edges for accidental objects or cropping. Write one precise correction if needed, such as restoring the original label position while keeping the new background.

Save the final image together with its prompt, references and selected model. Add critical text manually when exact lettering matters. Scientific figures need a separate expert review and real-data sources; a finished-looking image alone does not establish accuracy.
nano_site.guide.faq_2.question: What if a request appears stuck?
nano_site.guide.faq_2.answer: Keep its task identifier and check the existing status before submitting again. Save the error and request details if you need support; repeated submissions can create separate tasks.
nano_site.migration.faq_2.question: What belongs in a migration acceptance set?
nano_site.migration.faq_2.answer: Use representative generation and editing briefs, their original references, expected output settings and explicit pass criteria. Keep all raw results and record corrections and costs.
nano_site.versus2.title: Nano Banana 2.1 vs 2: Compare Your Image Workflow
nano_site.versus2.description: Compare Nano Banana 2.1 and Nano Banana 2 with a repeatable brief for text, reference edits, wide layouts and costs. No invented benchmark scores.
nano_site.versus2.heading: Nano Banana 2.1 vs Nano Banana 2
nano_site.versus2.intro: Decide whether to keep an existing image workflow or test a new model. Separate documented changes from results you have actually reviewed.
nano_site.versus2.section_0.title: Identify the two models before comparing
nano_site.versus2.section_0.body:
Google identifies Nano Banana 2 as gemini-3.1-flash-image and Nano Banana 2.1 as gemini-nano-banana-2.1. They are distinct models. Google describes 2.1 as an update with improvements in text rendering, visual quality and multi-turn consistency. These are vendor statements, not a benchmark performed by this website.

Record the exact endpoint used by your provider. A display name alone cannot establish which model produced an image. Our connected generation stays on fal; the controls and availability shown in this workspace determine what you can run here.
nano_site.versus2.section_1.title: Start with one brief and a visible pass rule
nano_site.versus2.section_1.body:
Use a job you already understand: a catalog image of a blue bottle, a poster headed “OPEN HOUSE”, or an edit that changes a background while preserving a character. Give both models the same text and the same reference files. Match shape and output size where both endpoints allow it.

Before generating, write what counts as a pass: the headline matches exactly, the bottle retains its silhouette, and nothing blocks the label. Avoid changing the prompt after seeing the first model’s output. Otherwise you are comparing two briefs as well as two models.
nano_site.versus2.section_2.title: Inspect the changes that matter to your work
nano_site.versus2.section_2.body:
Compare spelling at full size and at the final display size. Check faces, accessories and product edges against the reference. For a wide banner, look at repeated textures and seams across the full canvas. When revising an image, list the details that should remain unchanged and inspect them again after the edit.

Use a simple record for each output: model, task, spelling pass, preservation pass, layout pass, corrections needed and final usable file. Save unsuccessful examples too. One attractive image cannot tell you how reliable a model will be across your workload.
nano_site.versus2.section_3.title: Compare usable results and the complete cost
nano_site.versus2.section_3.body:
Record the quote before submission, the actual charge, the time to a usable download and any additional edits. Distinguish waiting in this site from waiting at the provider. If a request times out, check its task status before submitting another one; a duplicate request can incur another charge.

A higher first-request price may still fit your budget if it reduces corrections. A lower quote may fit simple tasks that already pass review. This page does not claim a measured speed winner or publish a fixed price ratio between the models.
nano_site.versus2.section_4.title: Switch in a small, reversible batch
nano_site.versus2.section_4.body:
Keep your accepted prompts and source files, then test a small set of representative tasks with the new model. Include at least one text layout and one reference edit. Compare the actual files before replacing the model in an automated workflow.

If 2.1 is awaiting connection or acceptance in this workspace, prepare the test pack now and run it when the named endpoint is enabled. Do not label another model’s output as a 2.1 result. Keep the old model identifier in saved task records so your comparison remains traceable.
nano_site.versus2.faq_0.question: Is Nano Banana 2.1 always better than Nano Banana 2?
nano_site.versus2.faq_0.answer: Google documents improvements, but this website has not published a controlled benchmark. Choose based on outputs that pass your specific brief and budget.
nano_site.versus2.faq_1.question: Can I reuse my Nano Banana 2 prompts?
nano_site.versus2.faq_1.answer: Use them as the first test input. Check endpoint parameters and inspect the result before adopting them in production; a saved prompt does not guarantee an identical image.
nano_site.versus2.faq_2.question: Does this page establish a shutdown date?
nano_site.versus2.faq_2.answer: No. Check the provider’s current model lifecycle notice for the exact endpoint you use. This comparison does not infer a closure date from a model update.
nano_site.versusGpt.title: Nano Banana 2.1 vs GPT Image 2.5: A Practical Test
nano_site.versusGpt.description: Plan a fair Nano Banana 2.1 vs GPT Image 2.5 comparison with matching inputs, a text-and-edit test pack, cost records and endpoint checks.
nano_site.versusGpt.heading: Nano Banana 2.1 vs GPT Image 2.5
nano_site.versusGpt.intro: Choose by the image task you need to finish. This guide explains a reproducible comparison; it does not claim that we have tested or connected both models.
nano_site.versusGpt.section_0.title: Match the specific endpoints, not just the names
nano_site.versusGpt.section_0.body:
fal lists Nano Banana 2.1 and GPT Image 2.5, with GPT Image 2.5 endpoints separated by workflow and variant. Its Flare text-to-image example uses openai/gpt-image-2.5/flare/text-to-image. Record the actual endpoint used rather than treating every GPT Image variant as interchangeable.

This website continues to use fal for model services. A comparison article does not enable a new model in the generator. Check the live model list and connection state before assuming either named model is available here.
nano_site.versusGpt.section_1.title: Build a three-task comparison pack
nano_site.versusGpt.section_1.body:
Task one is a product photo: one matte blue bottle on pale stone, side light and no added text. Task two is a poster with the exact headline “WEEKEND MARKET”, a large clear text area and no other lettering. Task three edits an authorised reference image by changing only the background.

For each task, save the same prompt and references for both endpoints. Select equivalent size and shape where possible; note unmatched options rather than hiding them. If a provider offers a seed, keep the recorded seed but do not expect a seed value to mean the same thing across different models.
nano_site.versusGpt.section_2.title: Score the file against the brief
nano_site.versusGpt.section_2.body:
Review product geometry, spelling, spacing, edge quality and any unwanted additions. For the reference edit, compare the subject before and after. A useful review sheet has one row for each constraint, with pass, fail or manual correction required; it does not need a made-up overall quality score.

Keep previews at the same display size and inspect each downloaded original. Repeating the test can reveal variable outcomes, but set a spend limit before running more samples. We have not measured a winning model for these tasks.
nano_site.versusGpt.section_3.title: Include edits, format and delivery in the cost
nano_site.versusGpt.section_3.body:
Record the current quote from the endpoint, the selected quality settings, output count and subsequent requests. Count how many images can actually be used after review. Provider billing and this site’s credits are separate, so a public API price cannot be copied directly into a subscription estimate.

If you need a transparent asset, inspect the downloaded file for an alpha channel and test it over a coloured background. A checkerboard painted into an image is not transparency. Confirm that the chosen endpoint exposes the required format before paying for the task.
nano_site.versusGpt.section_4.title: Make the choice for a repeatable workload
nano_site.versusGpt.section_4.body:
For catalog work, favour the tested workflow that preserves the product and needs fewer corrections. For posters, base the decision on exact text and layout. For reference editing, keep the model that meets the preservation list without rebuilding the subject. These are decision rules, not claims of model superiority.

Save the accepted prompt, settings, endpoint, date and result. Repeat the comparison when your workload or provider options change. Until both named endpoints have produced actual outputs, describe the result as a test plan, not a benchmark.
nano_site.versusGpt.faq_0.question: Which model renders text better?
nano_site.versusGpt.faq_0.answer: We do not have a controlled result for your text. Use the same headline and layout, then inspect every character and the final exported file.
nano_site.versusGpt.faq_1.question: Does this site provide GPT Image 2.5 generation?
nano_site.versusGpt.faq_1.answer: This comparison does not add a GPT endpoint. Availability is determined by the generator’s live model list and connected fal configuration.
nano_site.versusGpt.faq_2.question: Can I compare their prices using one fixed number?
nano_site.versusGpt.faq_2.answer: No. Endpoint, quality, output settings and later corrections affect the cost. Record current quotes for the same task and distinguish provider charges from site credits.
nano_site.mcp.title: Nano Banana MCP Guide: Evaluate Tools and fal Workflows
nano_site.mcp.description: Understand Nano Banana MCP and Claude workflows. Check an external tool’s identity, permissions, model endpoint, task status and billing before use.
nano_site.mcp.heading: Nano Banana MCP and Claude: choose a clear workflow
nano_site.mcp.intro: MCP can let an assistant discover and call tools. It is not an image model. This is an integration guide; this website does not offer an MCP server or an existing Claude connection.
nano_site.mcp.section_0.title: Know which part actually generates the image
nano_site.mcp.section_0.body:
An MCP host connects a client to a server that exposes tools and context. A Nano Banana image tool still needs a provider endpoint to generate the image. The assistant, MCP server and image provider are separate parts of the request.

Ask the tool operator to identify the server, the provider and the exact model endpoint. A label such as “Nano Banana MCP” is not enough to establish model identity, supported inputs or who receives your files. This site uses fal for its own model workflow; external tools have their own setup.
nano_site.mcp.section_1.title: Inspect the tool before installing or connecting
nano_site.mcp.section_1.body:
Read the tool’s documentation and repository if available. Check its maintainer, release history, installation command, host compatibility and privacy explanation. Confirm whether it runs locally or sends requests to a remote service, and where credentials and reference images are stored.

Use only the access needed for the task. A tool that creates one image should explain why it requests broader file or account access. Keep image generation credentials on a controlled server rather than in shared prompts, screenshots or browser code. Do not paste a provider key into an unknown chat tool.
nano_site.mcp.section_2.title: Define a server-side fal workflow
nano_site.mcp.section_2.body:
A proposed integration can accept a brief, model identifier, shape and permitted reference URLs. The server validates these fields, checks account rights and obtains a quote before submitting a fal task. The response should include a task identifier so the caller can follow status without creating another request.

Keep submission, status checking and result retrieval separate. If the connection breaks after submission, look up the existing task rather than automatically running the model again. This describes an implementation pattern; it is not a published MCP endpoint on this website.
nano_site.mcp.section_3.title: Separate drafting from a billable action
nano_site.mcp.section_3.body:
Let the assistant prepare a prompt and explain the selected parameters first. Before generation, show the model, references, output count and cost or spending limit. The user should be able to change the brief without triggering a paid request.

Start an external integration with a small non-sensitive test. Verify that an empty prompt is rejected, unsupported options are explained, errors include a task identifier where one exists and a retry does not create an accidental duplicate. Confirm what cancellation means for requests that are already running.
nano_site.mcp.section_4.title: Evaluate the returned file and keep a record
nano_site.mcp.section_4.body:
A successful tool response should identify the model and task, report the result state and provide a usable image link or authorised download. Open the actual file, verify its dimensions and inspect the brief’s important details. A chat message saying “done” is not enough.

Keep the prompt, endpoint, selected options and provider charge with your result. If you simply need to create and review one image, the normal generator workflow may be easier than installing an external connector. Choose MCP when tool discovery and repeatable assistant workflows solve a real need.
nano_site.mcp.faq_0.question: Can I connect this site directly to Claude through MCP?
nano_site.mcp.faq_0.answer: No MCP server or Claude connector is published by this site. This page explains how to evaluate external tools and design a server-side fal workflow.
nano_site.mcp.faq_1.question: Does MCP make image generation free?
nano_site.mcp.faq_1.answer: No. MCP is a connection protocol. The model provider can still charge for generation, and an external tool may have separate fees.
nano_site.mcp.faq_2.question: Where should the fal key live?
nano_site.mcp.faq_2.answer: On a server or another controlled environment used by the integration. Do not place it in public frontend code, shared prompts or an untrusted tool.
nano_site.logo.title: Nano Banana Logo Prompts: Create and Review a Mark
nano_site.logo.description: Prepare original Nano Banana logo concepts with a clear brief, reusable prompts and small-size review. Plan vector finishing and practical export checks.
nano_site.logo.heading: Nano Banana logo concepts: from brief to a usable mark
nano_site.logo.intro: Use image generation to explore a visual direction, then finish a clear, original mark. This workflow does not promise vector output or trademark eligibility.
nano_site.logo.section_0.title: Write a brand brief that describes your own product
nano_site.logo.section_0.body:
Name the audience, the product’s purpose and the feeling the mark should convey. Pick one recognisable idea, such as a curved peel forming a spark or a compact fruit silhouette with an unusual cut. Define where it must work: navigation, browser tab, profile image or product packaging.

Collect references for broad properties such as rounded geometry, restrained colour and flat shapes. Do not ask the model to reproduce another business’s emblem. Distinctive brand details should come from your own product and sketches.
nano_site.logo.section_1.title: Use a prompt with constraints you can inspect
nano_site.logo.section_1.body:
Try this original concept brief: “Design a flat symbol for an independent creative tool. One curved banana peel forms a small upward spark. Two simple colours, bold continuous silhouette, generous negative space, centred on a plain light background. No letters, gradients, shadows or existing brand marks.”

Generate the symbol separately from a wordmark so you can typeset the product name in a licensed font later. A request for a flat symbol is a visual instruction; it does not cause a raster image model to return an editable SVG.
nano_site.logo.section_2.title: Develop alternatives by changing one idea
nano_site.logo.section_2.body:
Keep the same brief and explore the silhouette, then the negative space, then the accent shape. Compare a peel-as-spark concept with a single-fruit concept before adding detail. Label the options by what changed, so feedback can be specific.

Avoid judging only large mockups. Place each candidate in a square crop, beside the actual product name and on both light and dark backgrounds. Eliminate concepts that depend on tiny highlights or a complex background to be recognisable.
nano_site.logo.section_3.title: Review at icon size and redraw the accepted design
nano_site.logo.section_3.body:
Check the candidate at 16, 32 and 64 pixels as well as a larger header size. Inspect whether the outline closes cleanly, internal spaces stay open and the symbol remains distinct in one colour. Test on real screens instead of assuming a large generated preview will scale well.

Rebuild the selected mark in an editable drawing tool when accurate curves and multiple sizes are required. Adjust geometry by hand and keep a source file. Automatic tracing can preserve unwanted bumps, so review the vector rather than accepting it without inspection.
nano_site.logo.section_4.title: Prepare an export pack with a clear source
nano_site.logo.section_4.body:
Keep the original design file, a reviewed SVG when you have created one, transparent PNG exports and a favicon set. Test transparency on a coloured background. Check that the header, browser icon and social preview use the same accepted mark.

Record the prompt, references and finishing changes. Review input permissions and applicable provider terms before commercial release. Original concept development does not guarantee that a mark is legally available or registrable; a formal brand launch may need a separate clearance review.
nano_site.logo.faq_0.question: Will the image model return a real vector logo?
nano_site.logo.faq_0.answer: Do not assume that. Check the endpoint’s output format. A flat-looking PNG is still a raster image; create and review an editable vector when the project needs one.
nano_site.logo.faq_1.question: How can I make a logo work as a favicon?
nano_site.logo.faq_1.answer: Start with a simple silhouette, review it at 16 and 32 pixels and remove small details that disappear. Export and inspect the actual favicon file.
nano_site.logo.faq_2.question: Does an original AI concept guarantee trademark registration?
nano_site.logo.faq_2.answer: No. This page is a design workflow, not a legal clearance or registration assessment. Review the finished mark and its intended market separately.
nano_site.blog.title: Nano Banana Guides: Prompts, Editing and Image Delivery
nano_site.blog.description: Practical Nano Banana guides for product photos, readable text, consistent characters, export dimensions and commercial-use review.
nano_site.blog.heading: Nano Banana guides for work you can finish
nano_site.blog.intro: Choose a guide by the problem in your image. Each article provides a concrete brief, a review method and a next step you can carry into the generator or editor.
nano_site.blog.section_0.title: Prepare a clear first request
nano_site.blog.section_0.body:
The product-photo guide turns a subject, background and lighting choice into a prompt you can evaluate. The readable-text guide separates exact wording from scene styling and explains when to finish lettering in an editable layer.

Start with the task closest to your project. Replace the example subject with your own, then write a short pass list before using credits. A prompt is useful when you can tell whether the output fulfilled it.
nano_site.blog.section_1.title: Keep the subject stable across edits
nano_site.blog.section_1.body:
The consistent-character guide explains how to build a small reference pack, list fixed details and review changes between images. Use it when a face, costume, mascot or product needs to remain recognisable across a series.

Treat reference roles separately: one image establishes identity, another may show lighting or pose. The editor workflow helps turn that plan into a precise change request. Availability and reference limits depend on the selected live endpoint.
nano_site.blog.section_2.title: Finish the file for its real destination
nano_site.blog.section_2.body:
The export guide explains pixels, aspect ratio, cropping and file formats so you can prepare an image for its final placement. The commercial-use and watermark guide helps organise source permissions, provider terms and delivery records.

These articles do not promise automatic publication approval or legal clearance. Inspect the actual downloaded file and the destination’s current requirements. Keep the accepted prompt, selected model and references with the finished asset.
nano_site.blog.faq_0.question: Which guide should I read first?
nano_site.blog.faq_0.answer: For a first image, start with product photos. For a problem in an existing result, choose the guide for text, consistency or export rather than rewriting everything at once.
nano_site.blog.faq_1.question: Are these guides evidence that every model is enabled?
nano_site.blog.faq_1.answer: No. Tutorials can be used to prepare a brief. Actual generation uses the live model list, connection state and quote shown in the workspace.
nano_site.blogProduct.title: Nano Banana Product Photo Prompts: A Reusable Brief
nano_site.blogProduct.description: Write product-photo prompts with a reusable subject, lighting and composition brief. Preserve references and review images before listing them.
nano_site.blogProduct.heading: Write a product photo prompt you can actually review
nano_site.blogProduct.intro: Begin with one product, one purpose and a short preservation list. The following examples are original prompt briefs, not images from a claimed model test.
nano_site.blogProduct.section_0.title: Define the product and its destination
nano_site.blogProduct.section_0.body:
A catalog thumbnail and a lifestyle advertisement need different framing. Write the final placement first: a square listing image, a portrait social post or a wide website banner. Then describe the product’s material, shape, colour and visible identifying details.

If the item already exists, use an authorised reference photo and list the features that must remain: label wording, cap shape, seams or component count. A text-only request creates an interpretation of the object; it cannot establish an exact match to a real product that the model has never seen.
nano_site.blogProduct.section_1.title: Use a short prompt with a clear hierarchy
nano_site.blogProduct.section_1.body:
Original catalog brief: “One matte cobalt-blue refill bottle, centred on a pale stone surface. Soft window light from the left, a short natural shadow, neutral background and generous space around the product. Straight-on camera at bottle height. No props, extra products or added lettering.”

For an authorised reference edit, replace the invented subject with: “Keep the bottle shape, cap, label and proportions from reference 1 unchanged; replace only the setting with the pale stone scene.” Tell the model which image defines the product instead of asking it to infer the role of each reference.
nano_site.blogProduct.section_2.title: Change the setting without rewriting the product
nano_site.blogProduct.section_2.body:
Lifestyle variation: keep the same bottle description and change only the setting to a quiet bathroom shelf with soft daylight. Campaign variation: use the same product and leave an uncluttered area on the right for later typesetting. Avoid adding several new effects in the same revision.

If the product shifts shape, return to the accepted reference and repeat the preservation list. Check whether the selected live endpoint supports the edit you need. Preparing a reference brief does not imply that generation is enabled or that every advertised model feature is exposed here.
nano_site.blogProduct.section_3.title: Inspect the image before using it in a listing
nano_site.blogProduct.section_3.body:
Compare silhouette, label, colour and functional parts against the actual product. Inspect reflections for invented logos or text, and make sure the image does not show accessories that are not included. Review the crop at its final size, not only in a large preview.

For exact packaging text, keep a clean image and typeset or composite the verified artwork in an editable layer. Save the approved prompt, references and file. Use the generator for a new scene or the editor for a targeted correction once the connection and quote are available.
nano_site.blogProduct.faq_0.question: Can text alone reproduce my real product exactly?
nano_site.blogProduct.faq_0.answer: It can describe the idea but cannot establish an exact match. Supply an authorised reference, name the fixed details and inspect the result against the real product.
nano_site.blogProduct.faq_1.question: Why does my product change during a background edit?
nano_site.blogProduct.faq_1.answer: The edit may alter more than the requested area. Make the preservation list explicit, use a clean product reference and reject outputs that change required details.
nano_site.blogText.title: Readable Text in AI Images: A Nano Banana Prompt Guide
nano_site.blogText.description: Plan exact wording, hierarchy and spacing in AI images. Learn how to inspect generated lettering and finish accurate text in editable layers.
nano_site.blogText.heading: Make text in AI images easier to check and finish
nano_site.blogText.intro: Decide the exact wording before styling the scene. A readable headline is a useful draft; final artwork still needs a spelling and layout review.
nano_site.blogText.section_0.title: Write the final words outside the image first
nano_site.blogText.section_0.body:
Create a text sheet with the headline, subheading and required details exactly as they should appear. Resolve capitalisation, punctuation and language before generating. If the image needs a date or price, obtain the confirmed value rather than asking the model to invent it.

Separate must-read information from decorative lettering. A poster can use one short heading and a quiet background without making the model handle an entire page of small type. Keep lengthy terms, addresses and legally required copy in an editable text layer.
nano_site.blogText.section_1.title: Prompt the layout as well as the words
nano_site.blogText.section_1.body:
Original poster brief: “A simple portrait poster for a community market. Exact headline: WEEKEND MARKET. Place it in a large, high-contrast area at the top with clear spacing between words. Below it, a restrained illustration of vegetables in a paper bag. No other text, logos or watermarks added as visible decoration.”

For a multilingual poster, provide the approved wording for each language separately. Describe which line is most important and where open space belongs. A request to add no decorative watermark does not remove a provider’s provenance marker or establish the downloaded file’s metadata.
nano_site.blogText.section_2.title: Proofread character by character
nano_site.blogText.section_2.body:
Compare the generated words to the text sheet. Check missing letters, repeated strokes, punctuation, accents, line order and spacing. Read the image at the size the audience will see, then inspect the original file for malformed characters.

If a short headline is wrong, request one targeted correction while preserving the rest of the composition. If the text keeps changing, switch to generating a clean background and add verified typography yourself. Repeating the same vague request is not a substitute for proofreading.
nano_site.blogText.section_3.title: Finish important typography in an editable layer
nano_site.blogText.section_3.body:
Place the accepted image in a design tool and add the exact text using a font you are allowed to use. Align margins, test contrast and check whether the smallest text remains legible at the final crop. Export a review file before making the final deliverable.

Keep both the image and the editable typography source. This makes later date, price or translation changes possible without regenerating the whole scene. The Nano Banana prompt library can help prepare the image brief; final text accuracy comes from the review and finishing process.
nano_site.blogText.faq_0.question: Does quoting exact text guarantee correct spelling?
nano_site.blogText.faq_0.answer: No. It makes the request clearer, but the actual output still needs a character-by-character check.
nano_site.blogText.faq_1.question: When should I add text manually?
nano_site.blogText.faq_1.answer: Use an editable layer for exact prices, dates, long copy, accessibility-critical information or lettering that has failed repeated generation review.
nano_site.blogReferences.title: Consistent Characters: Nano Banana Reference Image Guide
nano_site.blogReferences.description: Prepare character references, define fixed details and review a Nano Banana image series. Reduce conflicting instructions across poses and scenes.
nano_site.blogReferences.heading: Keep a character recognisable across image edits
nano_site.blogReferences.intro: A series needs a stable identity brief and clear reference roles. This guide helps you organise them and review each image; it does not guarantee perfect consistency.
nano_site.blogReferences.section_0.title: Build a small reference pack with a clear purpose
nano_site.blogReferences.section_0.body:
Choose an authorised front or three-quarter view that clearly shows the character’s face, silhouette and outfit. Add another view only when it resolves a detail the first image cannot show. Avoid collecting many images with conflicting hairstyles, proportions or costume designs.

Google’s 2.1 documentation describes support for up to 14 reference images. That official capability is separate from the limit of a particular fal endpoint or this website’s live controls. Use the accepted limit shown for the selected tool, and do not assume that more references always make a brief clearer.
nano_site.blogReferences.section_1.title: Separate fixed identity from the new scene
nano_site.blogReferences.section_1.body:
Create an identity list: face shape, hairstyle, outfit colour, emblem and key accessory. Keep it short enough to inspect. Then describe the variable scene, pose and lighting in a separate sentence.

Original reference brief: “Keep the character identity, short curved horns, teal jacket and round amber badge from reference 1. Change only the scene to a quiet station platform and the pose to holding a paper ticket. Preserve the character’s proportions. Do not add new accessories or alter the jacket emblem.”
nano_site.blogReferences.section_2.title: Make one controlled change at a time
nano_site.blogReferences.section_2.body:
Start from an accepted image and change the background or pose before requesting a different outfit, lighting and camera angle together. After each edit, compare the output to the identity reference. A chain of individually plausible edits can drift away from the original design.

If a result fails, return to the clean reference rather than using the mistaken image as the next identity source. Keep reference numbering explicit. When one file is a lighting example, tell the model it is not a replacement for the character reference.
nano_site.blogReferences.section_3.title: Review the complete series side by side
nano_site.blogReferences.section_3.body:
Place the images together at equal size. Compare face shape, hairline, costume, proportions and recurring accessories, then inspect hands and contact points. Judge whether the same character is recognisable without relying on a caption.

Record which image passed, what changed and what needs correction. Save the accepted reference pack with the prompt and model identifier. For images of real people, confirm permission to use their likeness and inputs before uploading; a prepared character brief does not supply that permission.
nano_site.blogReferences.faq_0.question: Should I upload as many references as possible?
nano_site.blogReferences.faq_0.answer: No. Use references that clarify a role and do not contradict each other. Follow the selected endpoint’s actual limits.
nano_site.blogReferences.faq_1.question: How do I fix a character that drifts between edits?
nano_site.blogReferences.faq_1.answer: Return to the clean identity reference, restate the fixed details and request one change. Avoid feeding a failed edit back as the definitive identity image.
nano_site.blogExport.title: AI Image Export: Resolution, Aspect Ratio and File Format
nano_site.blogExport.description: Choose AI image dimensions for web, social and print. Understand aspect ratio, pixels, cropping, transparency and final-file checks.
nano_site.blogExport.heading: Export an AI image for its actual placement
nano_site.blogExport.intro: Start with the destination’s width, height and format. Resolution labels are convenient presets; the downloaded file’s dimensions determine what you have.
nano_site.blogExport.section_0.title: Set the shape before choosing the pixel count
nano_site.blogExport.section_0.body:
Aspect ratio describes shape: 1:1 is square, 16:9 is wide and 9:16 is tall. It does not state how many pixels the file contains. Choose the ratio closest to the final placement so an important subject will not be removed by a later crop.

For a wide header, reserve the text-safe area in the brief and test how the image crops on a phone. For a product card, centre the item with enough space around the edges. Check the destination’s current upload requirements rather than assuming one export serves every placement.
nano_site.blogExport.section_1.title: Check actual dimensions, not just “1K” or “4K”
nano_site.blogExport.section_1.body:
Download the file and inspect width and height in pixels. A resolution preset can produce different dimensions for different aspect ratios or providers. Increasing a display density tag does not add missing pixel detail.

For a print example, a 6-by-4-inch image at 300 pixels per inch needs 1800 by 1200 pixels before bleed. The printer may specify a different density, colour workflow or margin. Confirm those requirements first; exporting a file labelled “4K” does not by itself make it print-ready.
nano_site.blogExport.section_2.title: Choose the format for the content
nano_site.blogExport.section_2.body:
JPEG is a common choice for photographic web images when transparency is unnecessary. PNG can preserve transparency and sharp graphic edges, while WebP can suit web delivery where the destination supports it. Inspect the exported file after compression, especially around small lettering and high-contrast edges.

When transparency matters, confirm an alpha channel and place the asset over two different background colours. A plain white background or a rendered checkerboard is not an actual transparent export. Select only formats available for the live endpoint, then make any needed finishing conversion in a suitable tool.
nano_site.blogExport.section_3.title: Keep an original and test the final crop
nano_site.blogExport.section_3.body:
Save the largest accepted original before resizing. Create separate delivery files for each placement, giving them clear names such as product-square and header-wide. Review the final crop at its intended display size and ensure text, faces and product edges remain intact.

After uploading, inspect the actual published image; a platform may resize or recompress it. Keep the source, prompt, model and export settings so you can prepare a different size without losing the approved version. Request higher resolution only when the use case and current quote justify it.
nano_site.blogExport.faq_0.question: Will changing DPI make a small image sharper?
nano_site.blogExport.faq_0.answer: Changing the density metadata does not create new image detail. Check pixel dimensions and the intended physical print size.
nano_site.blogExport.faq_1.question: Do I always need the highest resolution?
nano_site.blogExport.faq_1.answer: No. Choose dimensions sufficient for the final placement, inspect the result and consider the quote. Preserve an accepted original for later exports.
nano_site.blogRights.title: AI Images: Commercial Use, Watermarks and Review Records
nano_site.blogRights.description: Organise input permissions, provider terms, visible marks and AI image provenance before commercial delivery. Keep a clear record with the final file.
nano_site.blogRights.heading: Review AI image permissions and marks before delivery
nano_site.blogRights.intro: Commercial-use labels, input permissions and watermark behaviour answer different questions. Check each one for the actual provider, file and intended use.
nano_site.blogRights.section_0.title: Separate the provider’s permission from your inputs
nano_site.blogRights.section_0.body:
Begin with the current terms for the provider and account you used. Record the model endpoint and review date. A service’s commercial-use label does not establish permission to use a third party’s photo, brand asset, artwork or likeness as an input.

Keep a source list for uploaded references, including where they came from and what use was authorised. If the project involves a client’s unpublished material, confirm the upload and retention requirements before sending it to a provider. This guide is a workflow checklist, not a legal clearance.
nano_site.blogRights.section_1.title: Inspect visible branding and provenance separately
nano_site.blogRights.section_1.body:
A visible logo drawn in the image, a service-added overlay and an invisible provenance marker are different things. Google’s image-generation documentation states that generated images include SynthID. A clean-looking preview therefore does not prove that an image has no provenance marker.

Download the actual result and inspect visible marks, metadata and the destination’s disclosure rules. Do not promise “no watermark” without defining what was checked. This website does not offer a provenance-removal feature, and a prompt asking for no visible text does not establish the file’s marking behaviour.
nano_site.blogRights.section_2.title: Review what the image could communicate
nano_site.blogRights.section_2.body:
Check whether the output introduces a recognisable third-party logo, resembles an existing campaign, changes a product claim or suggests a person endorses something. Compare it to the approved brief and remove unintended details before publishing.

For ads and listings, verify prices, package contents and factual descriptions using the real product information. For a concept illustration, use a caption that describes it accurately. An accepted generation result still needs the same editorial review as other marketing assets.
nano_site.blogRights.section_3.title: Deliver the file with a usable record
nano_site.blogRights.section_3.body:
Keep the prompt, references, permission notes, model identifier, provider, creation date and important finishing changes alongside the approved export. Save the terms or a link and review date where your project process requires it. Avoid claiming that these records establish ownership or registration eligibility.

Before release, confirm the client’s delivery requirements, destination rules and any required disclosure. If the use raises a specific rights question, get an appropriate professional review. The goal is a traceable, reviewed asset rather than an unsupported guarantee attached to a download.
nano_site.blogRights.faq_0.question: Does “commercial use” mean I can upload any reference?
nano_site.blogRights.faq_0.answer: No. Provider output permissions do not establish rights to your input files or a person’s likeness. Confirm the relevant permissions separately.
nano_site.blogRights.faq_1.question: Does no visible watermark mean there is no marker?
nano_site.blogRights.faq_1.answer: No. Visible overlays and invisible provenance are different. Google documents SynthID for generated images; inspect the actual file and applicable delivery requirements.

workflow.product_description: Build a scene around your product while keeping its defining details.
workflow.product_hint: Upload your own product photo. Review labels, shape and materials after generation.
workflow.product_prompt: Use the uploaded product photo as the reference. Keep the packaging, label text, shape and material unchanged. Place it on a warm limestone surface beside a softly lit window, with realistic contact shadows and generous empty space for a headline. Do not invent a new logo.
workflow.character_description: Plan consistent portraits, outfits and scenes from a subject reference.
workflow.character_hint: Upload an authorized subject reference. Check identity details in each result.
workflow.character_prompt: Use the uploaded subject reference. Preserve the face, hairstyle and distinguishing features. Create a natural editorial portrait outdoors in soft morning light, wearing a plain olive jacket, with an uncluttered background. Keep realistic skin texture and hands.
workflow.social_description: Compose a clear focal point with room for your platform’s headline.
workflow.social_hint: Start with a draft, then check the crop and safe areas before publishing.
workflow.social_prompt: Create a horizontal editorial cover for a guide to growing indoor herbs. Show three small terracotta pots on a sunny kitchen shelf, fresh green leaves and a calm cream background. Keep the right third uncluttered for a title. No rendered text, no watermark.
workflow.poster_description: Arrange a readable message with a deliberate visual hierarchy.
workflow.poster_hint: Inspect every letter. Use further edits to correct spelling and placement.
workflow.poster_prompt: Design a vertical community workshop poster. Use the exact title "MAKE SOMETHING GOOD" and the subtitle "Saturday creative workshop". Deep green background, warm yellow lettering, generous margins and a small abstract paper sculpture. Make the title the strongest element. No additional text.
workflow.science_description: Draft diagrams with a clear structure and legible labels.
workflow.science_hint: Illustration drafts need expert review. Verify scientific relationships and every label.
workflow.science_prompt: Create a clean educational diagram showing the water cycle. Show evaporation from a lake, condensation in clouds, precipitation over hills and runoff returning to the lake. Use four labeled arrows, a white background, restrained blue and green colors, and no decorative text. This is an illustration draft for review.
workflow.logo_description: Explore a distinct shape before refining it into a finished brand asset.
workflow.logo_hint: Treat generated marks as concepts. Check distinctiveness and prepare final vectors separately.
workflow.logo_prompt: Explore a minimal logo concept for an independent plant nursery named "LEAF ROOM". Create a simple abstract leaf and doorway symbol with a distinctive negative-space opening. Use one dark green color on a plain white background. Include no mockup, texture, shadows or extra words.

studio_desk.T01.name: Image generator
studio_desk.T01.empty: Give your idea a first image
studio_desk.T01.hint: Describe one subject, its composition and lighting. Your real generated result replaces this starting view.
studio_desk.T02.name: Image editor
studio_desk.T02.hint: Name the change and what must remain unchanged. Compare the actual result with your source.
studio_desk.T03.name: Background remover
studio_desk.T03.hint: Inspect edges, hair and transparent materials against the checkerboard after processing.
studio_desk.T04.name: Background changer
studio_desk.T04.hint: Choose local colors or describe an AI scene. Use a cutout for local background composition.
studio_desk.T05.name: Product shadow
studio_desk.T05.hint: Tune softness, opacity and position. This is a local composition, with no generation charge.
studio_desk.T06.name: Relight
studio_desk.T06.hint: Select a lighting setup, preserve important materials, and inspect the real relit result.
studio_desk.T07.name: Object remover
studio_desk.T07.hint: Paint the object area on the source image. White regions are edited; black regions stay protected.
studio_desk.T08.name: Inpainting
studio_desk.T08.hint: Paint a region on the source, then describe its replacement. Keep the rest of the image protected.
studio_desk.T09.name: Image extender
studio_desk.T09.hint: Set the output boundary. The outlined source is a planning preview, not an already generated extension.
studio_desk.T10.name: Image upscaler
studio_desk.T10.hint: Choose a scale and compare the processed result against the original before exporting.
studio_desk.T11.name: Layers editor
studio_desk.T11.hint: Upload images as layers, then reorder, hide, lock and adjust each layer independently.
studio_desk.T12.name: Text on image
studio_desk.T12.hint: Write your headline, adjust color and size, then position it on the image.
studio_desk.T13.name: Canvas editor
studio_desk.T13.hint: Rotate, flip or crop the source with a live preview, then export your local composition.
studio_desk.T14.name: Batch processing
studio_desk.T14.hint: Upload several files. Local resizing creates a separate downloadable file for every completed item.
studio_desk.T15.name: Multi-size adaptation
studio_desk.T15.hint: Preview the selected output ratios together. Contain, crop and padding do not invent image content.
studio_desk.T16.name: Brand assets
studio_desk.T16.hint: Build a reusable name, palette, font and logo. The browser save action preserves this brand kit locally.
studio_desk.T17.name: Product image set
studio_desk.T17.hint: Choose the shots you need. Each submitted image has its own quoted charge and completed result.
studio_desk.T18.name: Bitmap to SVG
studio_desk.T18.hint: Upload clear artwork. Inspect the actual traced file before downloading it.
studio_desk.T19.name: SVG editor
studio_desk.T19.hint: Change the source and color, inspect its sanitized preview, then export the SVG at the selected width.
studio_desk.T20.name: Logo and icons
studio_desk.T20.hint: Start with a brand, industry and mark type. Only completed generated artwork is shown as a result.
studio_desk.T21.name: Start from template
studio_desk.T21.hint: Select a scenario and add your brand details before opening the matching generator.
studio_desk.T22.name: Sketch reference
studio_desk.T22.hint: Draw or upload a sketch and describe the final image. Sketch strokes become the actual request reference.
studio_desk.T23.name: Annotated edits
studio_desk.T23.hint: Draw arrows or boxes on the source and explain the numbered changes in your instruction.
studio_desk.T24.name: Prompt recipes
studio_desk.T24.hint: Write a reusable visual brief, separate private variables and copy a redacted version when needed.
studio_desk.T25.name: Continuous workflow
studio_desk.T25.hint: Review each operation in order. Processing begins only when you run the reviewed workflow.
